blocks.prompt: The Tube That Looks Back in Time
blocks.text: Long ago, people could only see the sky with their eyes. The moon was a smooth white circle. Then someone made a telescope. It was a tube with glass at each end. The glass bent the light and made far things look close. A man named Galileo pointed one at the moon. He saw that the moon was not smooth. It had mountains and round holes. He pointed it at Jupiter. He saw four tiny dots going around it. They were moons. Nobody had ever seen them before.

blocks.prompt: The Night Galileo Looked Up
blocks.text: In 1608, a Dutch glasses maker named Hans Lipperhey put two pieces of glass in a tube. Far away things looked close. People used it to spot ships coming into the harbor. A year later, in Italy, Galileo Galilei heard about the invention. He built his own, and he made it better. Then he did something nobody had bothered to do. He pointed it at the sky. What he saw changed everything people believed. The moon was not a smooth ball of light. It had mountains, valleys, and craters, like a world. The Milky Way was not a smudge of cloud. It was a crowd of stars, too many to count. And next to Jupiter sat four little dots that moved night after night. They were moons, circling Jupiter, not circling Earth. That mattered. People had been taught that everything in the sky went around Earth. Galileo's four dots said otherwise. A tube with two bits of glass had shown that the old picture was wrong.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A telescope's main job is collecting light, not magnifying
Refractor uses lenses. Reflector uses mirrors

blocks.prompt: Light Buckets
blocks.text: A telescope does two jobs, and the one most people think of is the less important one. Yes, it magnifies. But its real job is to collect light. Your eye has a pupil about seven millimeters wide when it is fully open in the dark. That tiny opening is all the light you get. A telescope mirror one meter across gathers roughly twenty thousand times more light than your pupil does. Astronomers call their instruments light buckets, and they mean it literally. The wider the bucket, the fainter the object you can catch. There are two ways to build one. A refractor uses a lens at the front to bend light to a point, which is what Galileo used. Lenses have a problem: different colors of light bend by slightly different amounts, so stars come out fringed. Isaac Newton solved this in 1668 by throwing out the lens. He used a curved mirror at the back instead. Mirrors reflect every color the same way, and a mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made enormous. Almost every serious telescope today is a reflector. Then there is the strangest part. Light travels fast, but not instantly. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach you, so you never see the sun as it is now. You see it as it was eight minutes ago. Point a big telescope at a distant galaxy and the light entering it has been traveling for millions of years. The galaxy may have changed completely since. A telescope is not really a magnifying glass. It is a time machine that only looks backward.

notes: Stars do not really twinkle. The air does it
Astronomers call atmospheric blur seeing

Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993
Adaptive optics reshape a mirror to cancel the blur
Webb's mirror is 6.5 meters of gold-coated hexagons

blocks.prompt: The Trouble With Air
blocks.text: Every star you have ever seen twinkle was lying to you. Stars do not flicker. They shine steadily. The twinkling happens in the last few thousandths of a second of the light's journey, as it crosses the moving air above your head. Pockets of warm and cold air bend light slightly differently, and they shift constantly, so the star's image dances. Poets like this. Astronomers do not. To them, twinkling means a blurred image, and they have a name for the problem: seeing. On a bad night of seeing, the largest telescope on Earth produces a picture no sharper than a small one. There are two ways out. The first is to leave. In 1990, NASA launched the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit, above the atmosphere entirely, where nothing bends the light before it arrives. The launch nearly ended in disaster. Hubble's 2.4 meter mirror had been ground to the wrong shape, off by about one fiftieth of the width of a human hair, and the first images came back blurred. Astronauts flew up in 1993 and fitted the telescope with corrective optics, essentially a pair of glasses. It worked. Hubble went on to become one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built. The second way out is cleverer and much cheaper: fix the air. A modern ground telescope measures the blur hundreds of times per second, usually by watching a bright star or a laser beam fired into the upper atmosphere. A computer works out exactly how the air is distorting the light, and a thin, flexible mirror behind the main one bends itself into the opposite shape, canceling the distortion out. This is adaptive optics, and it can make a telescope on a mountaintop rival one in orbit. So astronomers now do both. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, sits a million and a half kilometers from Earth with a 6.5 meter mirror made of eighteen gold-coated hexagons, chilled colder than 220 degrees below zero Celsius so its own heat does not drown the faint infrared light it hunts. Meanwhile, on ridges in Chile and Hawaii, mirrors bend themselves thousands of times a minute to undo the sky. Both are answers to the same complaint: the air is in the way.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Tube That Looks Back in Time

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Lipperhey filed the first telescope patent in 1608
Galileo's best telescope magnified about 30 times
Newton built the first reflector in 1668
A 10 meter mirror gathers about 2 million times more light than your eye
Hubble Deep Field, 1995: 3,000 galaxies in an empty patch
Event Horizon Telescope, 2019: dishes across Earth imaged a black hole's shadow

blocks.prompt: The Instrument That Made Us Small
blocks.text: For most of human history the sky was a ceiling. It was decorated, orderly, and close, and most cultures that looked at it built a story in which the Earth stood at the middle of things and everything else went around. The story was not stupid. It matched the evidence available, which was the naked eye. Then a Dutch spectacle maker named Hans Lipperhey filed a patent in 1608 for a tube that made distant things look near, and within two years the ceiling had fallen in. Galileo Galilei did not invent the telescope. He did something harder: he took an instrument built for spotting merchant ships and aimed it at the sky, which almost nobody had thought worth doing. His best instrument magnified about thirty times, less than many hobby telescopes sold today. It was enough. The moon turned out to have mountains that cast shadows, so it was a place, not a lamp. The Milky Way dissolved into individual stars, so the universe was deeper than anyone had drawn it. And four points of light shuffled themselves around Jupiter, night after night, obeying Jupiter and not us. That last observation was the dangerous one. It did not prove the Earth moved. It proved something smaller and more corrosive: that not everything went around us. Once one exception existed, the ceiling was just a hypothesis. Everything since has been an argument about size. A telescope's celebrated trick, magnification, is the minor one. Its real function is collection. The pupil of a dark-adapted eye is about seven millimeters across, and the light that misses it is simply lost. A mirror ten meters wide catches roughly two million times more. Astronomers speak, unromantically and accurately, of light buckets. This is why the history of astronomy is largely a history of grinding bigger glass: Newton replaced the lens with a mirror in 1668 because mirrors treat every color identically and can be braced from behind, and every serious telescope built since has been a variation on that decision. Bigger buckets bought something stranger than brightness. Light is fast but finite, so distance is duration. The sun you see is eight minutes stale. The light from a remote galaxy has been in transit longer than there have been humans to receive it, which means a large telescope does not observe the universe. It observes the universe's past, layered by distance, the far parts older than the near ones. In 1995 astronomers pointed Hubble at a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length, a patch deliberately chosen because it appeared to contain nothing at all, and left the shutter open for ten days. Roughly three thousand galaxies came out of the dark. The emptiest thing they could find was full. The instrument keeps changing what counts as a telescope. In 2019 a collaboration called the Event Horizon Telescope published an image of the shadow of a black hole at the heart of the galaxy M87. There was no tube and no single mirror. There were radio dishes scattered from Hawaii to Spain to the South Pole, recording the same faint signal at the same instant against atomic clocks, their data flown on hard drives to be combined into one virtual instrument the width of the planet. The picture was assembled, not seen. Four centuries on, the pattern has not changed. Each better telescope has demanded the same concession: we are further from the middle than we thought, and there is more of everything than we counted. The instrument was built to bring far things near. Its actual achievement was to move us out of the center and leave us there, looking.
